summary: For ages 9-10: round any whole number up to 1,000,000 to the nearest 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000 or 100,000. Keep the number-line 'nearer multiple' meaning central but scale it to large bounding multiples: identify the rounding place, read the single decider digit immediately to its right, zero everything after the rounding place, and handle halfway and cascade/boundary cases (e.g. 950,500 → 1,000,000). Link to estimating large sums and checking reasonableness.
misconceptions: Looking at the wrong decider digit or rounding to the wrong place.
Successive/chained rounding across places instead of one decision.
Losing place value in the unchanged trailing digits (they become zeros).

activities.title: Scaled rounding bench: drag across the midpoint
steps: Round 456,782 to the nearest 10,000: place it on a number line between the bounding multiples 450,000 and 460,000, with the midpoint 455,000 flagged.
Decide which multiple it is nearer and state the rounded value (460,000); check it against the midpoint.
Change the target place to nearest 100,000 so the line rescales to the bounding multiples 400,000 and 500,000 (midpoint 450,000), and round 456,782 again (it is past the midpoint, so 500,000).
After each decision, write out the rounded number and confirm every digit after the rounding place is now zero.
Explain which single digit you used to decide (the one immediately to the right of the rounding place) and why the rest are irrelevant.
activities.insight: Rounding a large number is the same nearness decision scaled up: the requested place chooses the two bounding multiples and the midpoint, the one decider digit settles the decision, and all trailing digits become zeros.

activities.title: Cascade and boundary cases
steps: Round 950,500 to the nearest 100,000, placing it between 900,000 and 1,000,000 with the midpoint 950,000 flagged.
Decide whether it rounds up (it is just past the midpoint) and work the carry explicitly: 9 hundred-thousands rounding up = 10 hundred-thousands = 1,000,000.
Try a case that sits exactly on a midpoint (e.g. 950,000 to the nearest 100,000), state the convention you are using (round half up), and give the result (1,000,000).
Explain in your own words what happens when rounding up rolls a 9 over into the next place.
activities.insight: When rounding up at a 9, the carry rolls into the next higher place; the rounded value can gain a digit (950,500 → 1,000,000), and this is still a single rounding decision, not chained rounding.

activities.title: Round to estimate a large sum
steps: Estimate 387,412 + 214,560 by rounding each addend to a sensible place before adding — for example, treat the numbers as two town populations you want a quick combined total for.
Round each number (e.g. to the nearest 100,000: 400,000 and 200,000) and add to get about 600,000.
State why the estimate is reasonable and how it could be used to check a full calculation (e.g. a budget total or population count).
Try estimating to a different place and discuss how the choice of place affects how close the estimate is.
activities.insight: Rounding supports quick, sensible estimates of large real quantities (populations, budgets) and a reasonableness check on exact answers; the chosen rounding place trades precision for simplicity.

activities.title: Consolidation: round to any specified place
steps: Given a six-digit number and a target place, state the two bounding multiples, the midpoint, the decider digit, and the rounded value.
Work a mixed set that includes a cascade trap (e.g. 950,500) and a halfway case.
Match several numbers to their rounded values for a stated place, and spot any that are not clean multiples of the target place.
Choose the place, then round — justify the bounding multiples the place implies.
activities.insight: Rounding to any place up to 100,000 becomes fluent and self-checked: the answer is always a clean multiple of the target place.

checkQuestion: Set the task and watch the working: 'Round 456,782 to the nearest 10,000. Now round 950,500 to the nearest 100,000. Then estimate 387,412 + 214,560 by rounding first.' Watch which column they use to decide and what happens at the boundary.
checkAnswer: 460,000; 1,000,000; and about 400,000 + 200,000 = 600,000 — deciding by the digit one place to the right of the rounding place, zeroing everything after it.
